utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday. I would like to greet Mr. Praljak, their counsels, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Prlic. I would also like to greet Mr. Stringer as well as Mr. Ferrara, and I would like to greet their associates. I would also like to greet everyone in the courtroom helping us in this case. We are going to carry on with the cross-examination, and I give the floor to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone else around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you should have the binder with you that we were working on yesterday, which was binder number 7, and we were looking at Exhibit P01187. And yesterday, when we left off, we were talking about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and if I recall correctly, you and I had agreed that -- first of all, that in early January of 1993, Mate Boban had signed off on the entire -- the entirety of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I think that was agreed sometime before the new year, that is to say, 1992, and that Mate Boban, on behalf of the Croatian delegation, signed everything that the international community placed on the table in the way of a peace agreement for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then also in January, and it's, I believe, the 10th, Mate Boban -- excuse me, Alija Izetbegovic signed off on the constitutional framework or the constitutional principles of Vance-Owen, but did not sign the map. Do you recall that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that this was a little different. He signed for the provinces which had a Croatian majority, or Muslim -- or Bosniak, rather, population majority, later on they were called Croatian and Muslim, but they were the majority provinces. And that there was some contentious details with respect to the separation and corridor through Posavina, as far as the Serb side was concerned. And as far as I remember, he said that he had signed the maps, but for a certain period of time, to force the Serbs to sign, too. And if they failed to sign, then I think they would start from scratch. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you'll go to paragraph 8 of this document that we're all looking at now, this relates to the resumption of the talks in Geneva on the 10th of January. And I'm going to move down to about halfway through that paragraph, and it's talking about the chairman, and that's, I believe, Vance and Owen, and it says: "They noted that Mr. Mate Boban of the Bosnian Croat side had accepted and signed the two agreements. President Alija Izetbegovic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had accepted the constitutional principles and the agreement dealing with the observance of a cessation of hostilities. He had not accepted, however, certain of the proposed provincial boundaries." And then it continues on to say that Radovan Karadzic of the Bosnian Serb side had deferred expressing his views. So, General, that's how it stood as of the 10th of January; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer, precisely what I said, some of the proposed boundaries. So with the Croats, there was no misunderstanding, and the separation and boundaries between the provinces or cantons with the majority Muslim population or Croatian population, there was no misunderstanding on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, that's not in the record, is it? I mean, you know, it's all or none on the boundaries, I would suggest to you. He didn't sign off on anything concerning boundaries; isn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that exactly. He didn't agree to some of the boundaries. He accepted others. So if he didn't accept all of them and didn't accept some of them, he did others. And I claim that he agreed to what was agreed between the Croats and Muslims, and as we know, there were negotiations and so on, and during those talks, and we have the transcript of the 15th of January with Vance-Owen, where the question was discussed; that is to say, the corridor or corridors were discussed mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then just to round this off, this being an agreement that was intended for three sides, we have no agreement whatsoever on the Bosnian Serb side. I think that we can agree on that, can't we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, they quite simply wanted a break and some time to state their views. So at that point in time, they didn't sign the agreement, but it wasn't an obstacle to continuing good cooperation between the Croats and Bosniaks. And let me mention once again that Mate Boban says, We're not in favour of war. We're not for war, he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next document is the plan itself. That's P09852.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document is that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 9852. General, this is the UN Security Council report of the Secretary-General. I should clarify, actually. This is the report of the UN Secretary-General on the activities of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, and it talks about the developments in Geneva during -- it's dated the 6th of January, 1993. And what I want to do is take you to some parts of this. And, General, you're not going to find the translation in Croatian in there. This is -- being one of the UN official documents, it's not a document that we've had translated, but we're not going to spend a lot of time on this. On page 2 of this, General, in paragraph 11, there's a reference to the draft map, constitutional principles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer. Are you now in binder 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, we're in binder 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I do not find it. Anyway, it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's probably toward the middle of the binder. It's one that I skipped over yesterday during the earlier part. 9852.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, General, on page 2 of this, in paragraph 11, it's just a reference to the draft map and the constitutional principles, and it's referring to those as annexes. And then on the next page, in paragraph 16, again there's a reference to an introductory part and annexes on the following points, and there are seven points there. Number 1 is: "Measures for achievement of an unconditional cessation of hostilities. "Measures for the restoration of infrastructure. "Measures on opening of routes. "Arrangements on the separation of forces." The fifth is: "Demilitarisation of Sarajevo." The sixth is: "Measures for monitoring borders of BiH." Number 7 is: "Return of forces to designated provinces." Now, General, I want to talk briefly about a couple of those. If you turn to one of the annexes, and this is on page 31 of the document, there's a sequence of events, and this is part of Annex 4 on the separation of forces. And the sequence of events there provides -- is laid out as follows: "A cease-fire, under the aegis of the overall cessation of hostilities." And let's just talk about these briefly as we go through them. An overall cessation of hostilities. Now, we know that Boban and Izetbegovic had signed off on the cease-fire, the cessation of hostilities, as of the 10th of January, 1993. But can we agree, General, that there was no overall cessation of hostilities because the Bosnian Serbs had not signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. The Bosnian Serbs, I don't know what they were doing at that point in time, but they didn't sign the document. And I don't know if they signed a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next one is: "Establishment and patrol of the demarcation line by the UN Protection Force personnel." Now, that aspect was not in place either, was it, by mid-January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, they needed to change the general function of the UN forces so that they could perform this job, and I know that Croatia, as far as Croatia is concerned, and the HVO too, they always sought assistance. And later on you saw this in Mostar. And if a truce was signed, that the third side should control and see that the cease-fire was adhered to and see who would violate it. Unfortunately, the mandate of the United Nations was not such that they could actually do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the third element of the sequence of events is: "Withdrawal of designated weapons systems of all parties." And by mid-January of 1993, that had not been achieved either; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, that wasn't achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to skip the last two elements of the sequence, and then I'm going to move to page 36 of this document. This is annex number 7 of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan from January 1993, and it says: "To enable the process of return to normalcy, and as a direct follow-on from the cessation of hostilities and the separation of forces, a return of forces to designated provinces will be conducted. This can start as part of the withdrawal of heavy weapons, but given the winter weather conditions, it is hard to fix a definite date for the completion of this process. We should, however, aim to achieve the return of forces within 45 days. "This stage will be coordinated with an agreed demobilisation of forces in being. "United Nations Protection Force/ECMM will monitor the withdrawal of these forces in conjunction with national and provincial authorities." So, General, according to the Vance-Owen Plan from January of 1993, a return of forces to designated provinces was contemplated, but it was only contemplated to take place within approximately 45 days after the agreement was signed by everyone, and that would take place as part of an agreed demobilisation under the monitoring of the UN. So my question, General, is to put to you that when the HVO HZ-HB, when Bruno Stojic, when Brigadier Petkovic, issued those orders and decisions we talked about yesterday on subordination and withdrawal of forces to designated provinces, they were actually jumping the gun because none of the conditions under Vance-Owen were in place for any of that to occur. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. Stringer. Let me repeat. It was signed with Mr. Izetbegovic or, rather, agreed, and what was envisaged here was what they did; that the forces that came from outside to certain provinces or cantons should go back to their original locations, and there was no reason for the plan, which was supported by the Croats and Muslims, should not be put into practice. And I remember that sometime on the 11th of May, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly adopted the Vance-Owen Plan. And as far as the Bosniak or Muslim side is concerned, they failed to act upon it, but launched offensive actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they weren't able to vanquish the Serbs. But, anyway, everything was in conformity with these demands and agreements and signatures under the auspices of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, what you're telling us, then, is that the decision and the orders on subordination and withdrawal of forces that we looked at yesterday, those were issued not pursuant to anything under the Vance-Owen Plan, but you're saying that was issued pursuant to an oral agreement reached in Zagreb with Mr. Izetbegovic; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described in very precise terms how that agreement came about, and what I do know is that it was within the frameworks of the things that had been signed, as far as the Vance-Owen Plan is concerned. So there was no reason for that part of the plan, whether the Serbs wished to sign or not - it was important for the international community and the development of the war and internal relations between the Croats and Muslims - that that portion of the plan, which was not contentious between the Muslims and Croats, should be put into effect, and that's logical, and that's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But what I'm asking you is, since we know that Izetbegovic only signed the constitutional principles and the cease-fire, what we know is that he did not, under the Vance-Owen Plan, sign off on a separation of forces agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, he agreed to the document which his defence minister published later on, Mr. Bozo Rajic. That's all I can say in answer to that question. And I don't agree that he didn't sign --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, again --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with respect to the cantons, the Muslim-Croat or Croat-Muslim majority cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, well, let's move on, then - you've made a reference to it already - to the transcript, the presidential transcript from the 15th of January, 1993, P01158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. Mr. Praljak, it had failed [as interpreted] to my attention, and I would like to thank the Prosecutor to put once again the stress on the Vance-Owen Plan. We have before us a document from the UN Security Council which is binding, because it's the report from the Secretary-General to the Security Council. It is an official document, and one cannot argue about those sorts of documents. In Annex 1 of this document, I see the composition and the various delegations, and I see that Mate Boban was accompanied by Mile Akmadzic and by Mr. Petkovic, and you have other delegations, of course. While listening to you, I seem to understand, but it only agreed, the penny only dropped a couple of seconds ago. Your version seems to be the following: You say that delegations signed documents, Izetbegovic and Mate Boban included, and you say the Serbs did not sign, but that's their problem. And you say that given that two delegations have signed, they are bound by those documents. And you are also adding that despite provincial or constitutional problems, it was stipulated in those documents that forces had to be subordinated to those that would be granted the monitoring or the management of provinces, and therefore it made sense that the HVO, where it had majority, controlled the BiH, and when the BiH was acknowledged as having the majority, take over the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or control the HVO. Correction from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is happening in early January, which would explain the document that -- Mr. Prlic's document that was characterised as an ultimatum by the Prosecution, and this would explain why Mr. Prlic is implementing what had been signed. Is that a fair summary of your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, entirely. It was a wonderful example for the two sides that had nothing contentious with respect to constitutional provinces, or the demarcation between the provinces and the Bosniak and Croatian majority cantons, to provide the basis for the international community to bring pressure to bear upon the Serbs. And anybody who wanted to join the plan seriously had to implement it fully, and that's how that document came into being. On the basis of this, the talks with Alija Izetbegovic, he accepted the document. I know there was a Jeddah conference, and I know how that was reneged. They sent a sort of ultimatum to the UN and said that unless they did this, acted upon it -- well, it's politics, but nobody's asking me about politics, so I won't go into that. Anyway, my answer to your question is, yes, you have understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So to summarise all this, the documents from the 15th of January, addressed to everyone, stating that some units had to be re-subordinated, according to you everything was cast in stone before the 15th of January, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. And let's not forget the contents, operative subordination of units, proportionality, mirror images, and everything else that it says there. No ultimatum and no desire to rule. You see that the 4th Corps says, Operatively, I accept Petkovic as being the HVO. There's no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But just to clarify, General, when we talk about what Izetbegovic signed in Geneva, he did not sign off on the separation of forces, number 1, isn't that true, in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he signed in Geneva. I know what it says he signed in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And part of that included the separation of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, that's not true, General. You're just making that up now. He signed off on the constitutional principles and the cease-fire. That's what the official documents tell us, and you don't know any differently, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that in Zagreb, they agreed upon a paper, and that includes separation of forces and establishing relations between the HVO forces and the BH forces and so on, and the negotiations went on for two days at the Hotel Esplanade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll get to that, but I'm talking about Geneva.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We also know, based on the documents that we've just looked at, that any separation of forces under the Vance-Owen Plan was only envisioned to take place when there was overall agreement among the three sides, that there would be monitoring involved by the UN, that it wouldn't be envisioned for at least 45 days because of the winter conditions, and so that really there is no separation of forces envisioned or in the works as between Croats and Muslim forces as of January 1993 under the terms of the Vance-Owen Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. Forty-five days was the dead-line, which didn't mean that they shouldn't begin. Now, of course, somebody who wrote about that knows -- anybody who wrote about that knows that you need time for certain things, but you start anyway and then carry them out within a 45-day dead-line. Now, what the Serbs were going to do here was immaterial. What was important was to decide upon what was signed, and that was the agreement signed by the Croats and the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so when we were talking about Gornji Vakuf and the HVO's demands on subordination or departure of ABiH units, in the case of Gornji Vakuf they were given five days, which is wholly unrealistic, isn't that true, even if the ABiH were inclined to do it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The situation was already calm down there, and it wasn't that the BH Army was asked to withdraw, but according to this agreement, just the brigade from Jajce, which according to that same agreement later on did leave the area and returned to another province.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's look at the presidential transcript here, P01158. And I want to take you to some remarks beginning with President Izetbegovic on page 48 of the transcript. He starts off by saying: "I will just take the floor ..." And just for the record, as I think everyone knows, this is a meeting in Zagreb at the Presidential Palace on the 15th of January. Tudjman, Izetbegovic, Boban, Susak, as well as Vance and Owen are present at this meeting. And on page 48, Alija Izetbegovic begins by saying: "I will just take the floor once more, and I won't take it again. I would say I agree with President Tudjman, that this discussion should be finished. But I think it is necessary to resolve a misunderstanding here because I think it may be at the core of the fighting that has now happened in Gornji Vakuf, a misunderstanding, perhaps a misinterpretation of these documents." And moving down, I'm going to skip over a few sentences, he's talking about interpretation, and he says: "Mr. Boban said he understood from these papers that the armies -- that each army should withdraw to their territories. That's not how I understood the papers, and I don't know whether this was the intention of these documents. "Because I do not see that they define who has what territories, whose armies these are, you know. So I'm afraid what is now going on in Gornji Vakuf may have been caused by a misunderstanding of this item of these agreements. "I am not sure I understood Mr. Boban correctly, but he seems to have understood that, say, now that the Bosnian Army should withdraw from the region, from the Travnik provinces now, and the HVO should take it over completely. I did not understand these papers like this." And then President Tudjman asks a question about the Serbs. Izetbegovic continues, and he basically indicates that, yes, there will be such moves at some time in the future, but the moment for that has not yet been set. He says: "I'm afraid that such a reading of these papers or this provision, and Mr. Boban, that such a reading may have caused the clashes in Gornji Vakuf because he wants the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to withdraw from there now, but since it is not doing so, then it should be driven out." And Boban says: "No, that's not how things are set up." Izetbegovic says: "I think because you, Mate, said it a few moments ago, hasn't withdrawal been foreseen?" And Boban says: "I said you should sign the document. Tell your people that provinces 10 and 13 have been agreed on between the Croat and the Muslims, and there won't be any problems for you to do it like I did on TV." And he continues. Izetbegovic: "I don't think this was foreseen in any of these proposals. It was not foreseen that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina should leave either the Travnik province or Mostar. That's not how I understood these papers. I'm not sure that's what is written there. It seems to me, I'm sorry, Mate, that is how you understood it. "If that's now how you understood it," Boban says, "that's how I understood it."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the right page displayed on screen. Could the document read please be put on the screen so we could cite interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yeah, It's okay. [Interpretation] Okay, we'll start again. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the record, in the transcript I just finished reading from page 50, and now we're going to move to page 51, if the technical people could move us to page 51 so the interpreters can read along. And then Gojko Susak makes a statement, and we can all read the first paragraph. He's talking about areas where there are predominantly Muslim troops, or dividing the command, and then in the second paragraph it says: "I cannot understand what's now contentious in this, to have a common interest to defend ourselves against our common enemy. Isn't that the part we have achieved? I sat with you in the room, in the hotel, here, at the Esplanade, when we made a gentlemen's agreement that you would work on this. I don't see what's contentious if, in Gornji Vakuf, no matter if there are more Muslims or fewer Croats there, but it is in the territory controlled by the HVO, if orders now coming from Sarajevo are contradictory to orders from Mostar. Well, you're killing yourselves, then the Serbs do not need to fight you any longer. "Thank you very much." And just to continue a little bit longer, I'm going to move down to the remarks of David Owen. He says: "I think this has been a very useful discussion, although we have not reached any definite conclusions. I think the one and only real way to reach any solution is by discussing these issues. "With regard to individual provinces, I said, while explaining the system, that the Serbian military forces would withdraw to the provinces of Banja Luka, Bijeljina, and Eastern Herzegovina. "I did not make any suggestions about the others, but I think I mentioned that this was an issue for the BH Army and the HVO to discuss together. "In any case, the discussion we have just attended is a good illustration of the urgency of reaching agreement together. I understand that commanding or the command should be determined according to majority representation." Now, I'm going to stop there, General, and just put a couple of questions to you based on this. Because isn't it true that what this -- well, first of all, in terms of the timing, this is the 15th of January, 1993; this is a discussion that's taking place at 1550 hours in the afternoon, almost 4.00 in the afternoon. So this discussion's taking place, General, after you've already left Zagreb and are heading down to Mostar with the text of this alleged oral agreement or gentlemen's agreement that you've been telling us about; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But what we see in this discussion is that, in fact, there is no agreement on this text, and the closest that we get to an agreement is what we learn from Gojko Susak; that there was a gentlemen's agreement that Izetbegovic would work on it. Now the fact is, General, that no president, not even Izetbegovic, who I know you are critical of in many ways, no one's going to agree to such a broad sweeping agreement on subordination, separation of forces based upon an oral gentlemen's agreement that's made in a hotel. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. For the most part, agreements were reached in hotels because that was where Izetbegovic was based. Gojko Susak over in Esplanade Hotel says, We agreed on this as human beings, and you should work on it; we agreed that this should be implemented. And it's quite correct what Mr. Izetbegovic is saying here -- there is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Break taken at 9.55 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we've gone through this text. I've read a lot of it out. We can all read it. We can draw our own conclusions from what's being said. Let me just, to round this off, put a couple of points to you. First of all, what the text tells us here, General, is that as of the late afternoon hours -- the late afternoon hours of the 15th of January, this so-called agreement, this text that you claim existed or was reached with President Izetbegovic, in fact, was no agreement because clearly parties here are talking about something other than an agreement; they're talking about negotiations, et cetera. So that's number 1, there was no agreement, as you claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a question or is this a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to the general to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Simply that as is indicated, after reading this, General, the fact is, I'm putting to you, that despite what you claim, there was no agreement on separation of forces reached at the Esplanade Hotel. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was an agreement that was reached there. Gojko clearly says, We agreed on that as human beings. Lord Owen agreed with that understanding of command and minority -- a majority representation. What General Petkovic said in Travnik and elsewhere at the levels of brigades and operative zones of the BH Army brought 60 per cent of the manpower to the front-lines, it had a 60 per cent share in the command -- 80 per cent -- 80 per cent share. Separation of forces, that's what it's about. It's not about separation of forces on a 45-day dead-line between the BH Army and the HVO, but rather the VRS, on the one hand, and the BH Army and the HVO, on the other, and it's not about leaving the BH Army but, rather -- the BH Army units, but rather leaving those units that came to certain areas from a different area, causing unrest. Everything is crustal clear. This was a perfect example of the fair attempts to put a stop to the conflict and to reach an agreement between the Croats and the Muslims on the Croatian part, and I hope the honourable Judges will go through all of this transcript in its entirety in order to make sure and see clearly who was in favour of peace and who was in favour of fighting on. I agree with nothing whatsoever that you have just put forward, Mr. Stringer. That is not what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's see if we can agree on one final point on this. Any head of state -- or I should say no head of state, not even Alija Izetbegovic, would agree to such a broad, sweeping, and important agreement and its implementation without signing off on a written version of it; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The written version was signed by his army minister, Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's the Bozo Rajic who testified earlier in this case as a Defence witness? Oh, no, I apologise, that's -- I'm wrong on that. This is Bozo Rajic, who was a Croat member of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Let me try a third time. We're all having a bad day in this courtroom, Mr. President. This is Bozo Rajic, who was a Croat. He was the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't think I'm having a particularly bad day, myself, come to speak of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you invoked Lord Owen here. And just again to clarify his remarks, what he said here about a separation of forces is that he suggested, and I'm looking at page 52 of the transcript, he says that -- while explaining the system that the Serbian military forces, Serbian military forces would withdraw, he says: "I did not make any suggestions about the others." And so, again, just to clarify, we don't have any agreement or suggestion by Lord Owen that there's any agreement on a separation of forces as between HVO and ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says, I've not put forward any suggestions. Rather -- and I think he means, I noted that this was a question to be resolved by the BH Army and the HVO. There is nothing being said about the separation of forces. Rather, on page 53 he realises that command -- or, rather, the command must be determined based on the principle of majority representation. He is speaking here of military representation, of course. Go to the front-line, gentlemen, fight if you like, and then, if you like, you can go on and take all of the commands in their entirety under your control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm ready to move to the next binder, unless there are questions from the Chamber on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, let me return to this Vance-Owen Plan. Earlier, I summed up your position, which you have developed at length. The Prosecutor asked you a few questions on that also, and you maintained your position. Now, my difficulty is as follows: When talking about an agreement or a plan that was signed, I don't have it here at hand, so there's these plans and discussions held in Geneva that were eventually signed? General Petkovic will come and testify, and we can revisit the question at that time, because he was there and he can tell us exactly. I hope, at least, he can tell us exactly what happened. But since I don't really know which documents were signed, well, in the document shown by the Prosecutor on the meeting that was held after the Geneva conference, document P9852, we have Annex 7, and I wish -- maybe it would be good to have it on the screen. And Annex 7 is on the return of forces in designated provinces. This is an official document, it is Annex 7, it is part and parcel of the negotiations, and it stipulates that as of -- well, there's going to be a sequence with three steps. First step, cessation of hostilities. Second step, according to the document, separation of forces. Third step, return of forces. And if I understood things correctly, returning the forces to designated provinces will lead to re-subordination. Now, I would like to know whether the document you claim to have been signed is Annex 7. Is it that; yes or no? I don't know. Whatever the case, Annex 7 is a document that is annexed to the plan, and everyone can take a look at it. Now, here are my questions, General Praljak: According to you, was this the sequence of events: cessation of hostilities; second, separation of forces; thirdly, return of forces to designated provinces? Was that the sequence of events planned, because this is what I have on Annex 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the information I had at the time, yes, that was exactly what was envisaged. The 45-day period was in relation to the Serbs, and the return of the forces was also about the Serbs. What they took they had to give back, based on the maps that were tabled. The BH Army and the HVO had this agreement about setting up a joint command at the levels of operative zones and brigades, based on the proportions of soldiers along the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the binder, we see a document that Mr. Stringer did not mention. Maybe he wanted to use it, but he didn't have enough time. The document has already been tendered, and I would like to talk about it. I would like to see it on the screen. It's 3D00320. The spokesman of the conference is having a press conference in order to explain what exactly was signed. Registrar, could we please have this document on the screen, 3D00320.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to inform you, I deliberately skipped over that one. The plan was to come back to it because it relates to March. In any event, I'm going to come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is not the document. You must have made a mistake, Mr. Registrar. This is not the document that I have under 3D00320.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can assist, 3D00320 is a very large document, and if you can just give me a moment, I can direct the Registrar to the page -- the specific pages that would have been placed in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If this means that there is a short break, I would like to use it to come back to the last answer you have given, Mr. Praljak. With regard to Annex Number 7, you seem to have said that this withdrawal/return of forces only applied to the Serbs. Could you confirm that that's what you meant, and if so, could you explain how come? What's the reasons for this restriction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because based on the Vance-Owen Plan, the Serbs were supposed to withdraw from large portions of the territory that they had previously taken. Their forces from those territories that they had taken were supposed to go and join the majoritarian [as interpreted] Serb forces, based on the Vance-Owen Plan. As far as the BH Army is concerned, only those units that came as the Jaganjac Brigade were supposed to go back to their own original position. Therefore, all the BH Army unit positions in Mostar would remain the same, as well as in Konjic, Jablanica, and everyone else, same as applied to the HVO in Tuzla, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I just look at the document, and I find nothing of what you have now said in Annex Number 7. It's simply not there, and I wonder where you take this information. You have stressed that you have not been in Geneva, as we know. I don't understand why we should -- why we should accept this explanation of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the explanation that I know was the reality. Only the Serbs could have withdrawn. We did not take control of any territory from which we were to -- should withdraw, according to the maps and the Vance-Owen agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I could have imagined that you would say the ABiH would have to withdraw from Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because we're proposing a joint command, and if the BH Army has units up at the positions, then in Gornji Vakuf they will have as much command as they have units, and that's crystal clear in the proposal; reciprocity with respect to the number of soldiers that the BH Army or HVO have on the ground. And had that been implemented consistently, then the BH Army would have been in command of the Bosnian canton, Travnik and so on, because it had more soldiers, had it positioned them up at the front-line facing the Serbs. And that follows quite clearly from Mr. Stojic's and Mr. Petkovic's texts. That was the agreement that was reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am talking about Annex Numeral 7 to the Vance-Owen Plan, which presupposes, first, follow a cessation of hostilities, if there's a cessation of hostilities. And that, of course, refers also to Serbs, that's not only meant between Muslims and Croats. Then I don't see why the Muslims should not withdraw from Gornji Vakuf and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I support what my colleague is saying. The question that my colleague asked, I could have asked it myself. This text of Annex 7 applies to all three parties, and not especially to the Serbs. This is how we read this text. And, General Praljak, you seem to say it only applies to the Serbs. This document does not state that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the unnecessary microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying how the document was interpreted, Your Honours. How can you propose a joint command if the forces are going to withdraw? I just don't see it. I don't see the logics of a joint command in Mostar if we say that the BH Army should leave Mostar. That wasn't the intention. The BH Army and the HVO were two -- or, rather, one army with two components.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, this your interpretation. I would like to go back to the document, and Mr. Stringer wanted to help me by giving me the document 3D028-0825; isn't that the right number for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The page numbers for the English -- I don't have the document in the court with me because I took it out of my own papers for later, but I believe we're at 3D -- this the page number of the document now, 3D28-0325 for the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the general's version, it would be page 3D12-0239. That's in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, on the 25th of March, 1993, two months after January, the spokesperson makes the following statement. He says that President Izetbegovic and Boban signed together this document; namely, the map and the agreement on temporary power. So this is the spokesperson doing that. And then we learn that the delegation, headed by Karadzic for the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had not signed the plan and had gone back home. And when you turn the page, you see that there is a statement made by the delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, reiterating that they have signed this, but that their signature would only be valid if some conditions were met. So this is not very clear. We are aware that some parts were signed, but others are put back into question. So my question is the following, General Praljak: Did you know that the spokesperson had made this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read this statement in the papers, and it was generally discussed. I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to go back to P1158, which is this meeting of the 15th of January in Zagreb. This document may be interesting because all participants were there, but on top of that we have Lord Owen, and we have Cyrus Vance, so all stakeholders were there, and what they're going to say will be very interesting indeed. This is why I would like to have on display page 20 of the English version, please. Page 25, correction, page 25, and Lord Owen is taking the floor on this page. Page 25. Lord Owen is going to take the floor, following an intervention from Mr. Izetbegovic, on the fact that some zones or areas were subject of ethnic cleansing during the conflict, so he's mentioning this. And we seem to understand that Mr. Izetbegovic is asking himself some questions, because he seemed to say, when you read his statement, that one cannot accept that just because some territories were won through ethnic cleansing, they should be retained. So Lord Owen is taking the floor on this very important topic, and on page 25 it starts with, first of all, he's going to talk about a plan for the withdrawal of forces. And what I'm saying to myself is that if he's mentioning this, it means that there is a plan for the withdrawal of forces, because this is mentioned on the 15th of January. He's not going to state that out of the blue. So he says that there is a plan for withdrawal of forces. So, General Praljak, what Lord Owen is saying here, do you think that he is actually talking about those agreements that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to all my information, based on my talks about it, that's what that was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So according to you, he's mentioning those agreements. Very well. So if you allow me, we will move to page 37 of the same document. And on this page, we see that Mate Boban is taking the floor. Mate Boban is mentioning what Lord Owen has just said. He talks about clashes between the Muslim and Croatian armed forces, and he says the following: The answer to all this is in signing a general package. General Praljak, Mate Boban talks about the signature of the package. I was wondering whether he includes all the sequence of events; the cessation of hostilities, separation of forces, return of forces in designated provinces, and re-subordination according to the majority rule. The word used in English is "package." I'm not sure what it says in your own language. I was wondering whether it included the entirety of the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the talks that I participated in at the time, and according to the text that was written, it is precisely as you have interpreted it, to the best of my knowledge then and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm suggesting an interpretation. I'm not saying that it is my own interpretation. It's an assumption I submit. I put that to you. I will conclude with page 53 of the same document. David Owen summarises the discussion, and he says that the ABiH and the HVO should carry on talking to each other. But what I find rather interesting is that he talks about President Tudjman. It says: "Perhaps President Tudjman ...," and so on and so forth. And Mr. Owen says that President Tudjman could actually be a middle person in this. And this caught my attention, because it says that President Tudjman could serve as an arbiter, and in a debate that includes Boban and Izetbegovic, it seems that the choice of an arbiter would be Tudjman, and he points out the various grounds for this. He says that it's a man of considerable experience, so he seems to want President Tudjman to play a role in solving all this. So according to you, are you rather surprised or not, first of all, that President Tudjman would serve as an arbiter and, secondly, that President Tudjman could solve the problem while Mr. Izetbegovic is also there? Why do you think Mr. Owen is choosing Tudjman as an arbiter? This is an assumption, because of course the sentence starts with "Perhaps." But I'm sure that when he's saying this, he's obviously making a position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours and Judge Antonetti, because Franjo Tudjman, in political terms, had a political relationship towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, both towards Muslims and Croats, he behaved the same way, he approached them in the same way, both with respect to the distribution of weapons, taking in the wounded, recognising Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we see an understanding of the problem on the previous pages. He understands that there were one and a half million Serbs there in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there were another 500.000 Serbs in Croatia, and he says to Alija Izetbegovic, Don't continue waging a war; you'll destroy yourselves and you'll destroy Croatia, and we don't want to vanquish the Serbs, actually, we just want to arrive at a just solution. So you have to read this document in its entirety and other documents, too, to see that the position taken by Franjo Tudjman, as far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, was not on the side of the HVO, but a just solution to the problem, which was a very complex one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will conclude, because the question of my colleague on Gornji Vakuf is an important one and I would like to go back to it in order to understand this very clearly. My assumption is the following: Let's take any given province or town, and this province is controlled, militarily speaking, by the opposite side. According to the Vance-Owen Plan, this province, still speaking from a military point of view, would be ruled by the side that was in an inferiority position because it had to surrender. According to you, does that mean that the Vance-Owen Plan would mean that those who have won must leave and those who lost should stay because they were the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. They asked that 24 per cent of the territory, to begin with - and that is stated in the transcript earlier on - that the Serbs -- well, the Serbs were required to withdraw from 24 per cent of the territory that they had control of until then, and even more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you're talking about the Serbs. I'm talking about the Croats and the Muslims. I'm leaving the Serbs aside for the time being. I give you the example of a region which is occupied, say, by the HVO, but this region, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, should be managed by the Muslims. Does that mean that the HVO has to withdraw, has to leave, and that the army on the ground will be the ABiH, and does that mean that the military units of the HVO will be subordinated to the ABiH? Is it how things have to happen, or does that mean, as you said, that there will be a joint command of forces on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't need to leave, neither the HVO forces from the majority Muslim provinces nor members of the BH Army from the Croatian majority provinces, but to set up a joint command proportionately. So nobody needed to send the HVO forces from Tuzla, Zepce, and so on, or vice versa. They should remain there and were to remain there, as they did do, in fact, until the end of the war, under the command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you're adding another concept. Every time, there's something new that crops up. You have just said that it's a joint command, but with proportionality. This is what you just said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Crystal clear, that's what it says, proportionate. As many soldiers one component has and takes to the front-line, in this case facing the aggressor, the Army of Republika Srpska, let them take an equal number from the brigade command and so on. That's very fair, very just, and very clear. That's what the American Army did, for example, when it liberated France. That's how armies act today; proportionate command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your position will be in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... now entered NATO, it said precisely which of its men should hold what NATO positions for it to be viable, and that's how it's always done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Stringer, I have no further questions regarding this document. But as you understood, I am eagerly waiting Mr. Petkovic to touch upon those issues once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to stay with the document that the President has gone to, I was going to do this later, but since we have the document in front of us, let's do it now. This is, again for the record, 3D00320, and so again this is not January 1993 now. We've moved ahead to early March of 1993. I'm sorry, the 25th of March, 1993. And, General, I want to direct your attention to document number 103 as part of this, which is the next document, obviously, in the English version, the next page of the document in e-court. And, General, do you have document 103 there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in your version -- or the original language version, could you read out for us the title of document 103?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vance-Owen Plan: The conditions set by Alija Izetbegovic for signing the Vance-Owen Plan -- the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. New York. The 25th of March, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "The conditions." Now, just for the record, General, your people forgot to translate the rest -- or the full description of the document number 103. In the English version, it's listed as simply "Vance-Owen Plan," and it does not have the rest of the part about the conditions. And so I think that's an important correction that should be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with my learned friend Mr. Stringer, but I have to say that the translation of these documents was done by the CLSS, the official service, and not by the Praljak Defence and his team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, looking at these conditions, I want to direct your attention to item number 2, where they say that: "Our signatures on the proposed document will become invalid, and we shall consider them void if the following conditions are not met: If all sides, and especially the aggressor, do not sign the proposed documents without any amendments or conditions within a reasonable time-frame ..." And then it continues. The reference to the international community and, thirdly, if the aggression continues. So, General, can we agree that, in fact, all sides did not sign the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, it never happened, and that the Serbs had a referendum -- the Vance-Owen Peace Plan failed and the Serb side never signed the agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. However, the Croats did sign, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we know that. And so according to this, then, the signature from the Muslim side, then, would have been invalid, in that the Serbs did not agree to the plan within any reasonable period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the conditions which they say should be accomplished in the future. And what the future looked like, well, the Prlic Defence has presented that here in court. I know that the BH Assembly, on the 11th of May, adopted the Vance-Owen Plan, and that in order to defeat the aggressor, firm military agreements had to be reached with the Croats, as with the Republic of Croatia, like in 1995, to attack the Army of Republika Srpska, and not the Croats along the Western borders, as Sefer Halilovic put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in item 3, another condition states that: "None of the provisions of the signed documents can be interpreted or understood as deviating from the sovereignty of BH as an independent and indivisible state entity." Now, General, wouldn't that interpretation of Vance-Owen be contrary to the establishment of an autonomous Croatian area that you wanted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, an autonomous Croatian area is already contained in the constitutional provisions about the cantons. But with the signing of the Vance-Owen Plan, the disintegration of Bosnia-Herzegovina began, or -- and you have my talk with Mr. Jaganjac, where I say the HZ-HB, with the signing of the Vance-Owen Plan, no longer existed. So let's set in order what we can within the frame the Vance-Owen Plan, and that was the politics followed by Franjo Tudjman and Prlic, who took part in the creation of -- well, the political background, but unfortunately Alija Izetbegovic slowed that down and obstructed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm ready to move to the next binder of documents now, Mr. President. This is binder number 8. If I could have just a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you -- I want to follow up a little bit on something we talked about briefly during an earlier phase of your cross-examination. General, you're aware that in late June of 1993, General Petkovic issued an order requiring that all Muslim men -- military-aged Muslim men within the zones of responsibility of the North-West and South-East Herzegovina Operative Zones be arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to that question. The order that Mr. Stringer has prepared clearly indicates that it relates to the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, so I'd like you to interpret that order as an order sent from the north-west, North-West Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, are you aware that throughout July and August of 1993, HVO forces, armed forces, in the North-West and the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zones arrested and detained large numbers of Muslim men of military age?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was done over a period of two months, that's what you say. I can't agree with that. When I arrived on the 24th, I don't know that there was any disarmament of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, General, you're telling us that prior to the 24th of July, you had no knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No direct knowledge, none. I knew certain things; that there had been an act of treason and so on and so forth, but I didn't know anything else because I spent that time in Boksevica, and after that in Zagreb, and after that I dashed off into the fighting in Vakuf, and the whole story was beyond the boundaries of my mind and time back then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Correction for the transcript. Page 18, line 18, the general said, Mr. Stringer, you reduced that to a two-month period, and not that it was done over a two --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: One speaker at the time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, based on what you told us already, when General Petkovic handed over command of the HVO Main Staff to you on the 24th, he didn't tell you anything about the arrests of Muslim men throughout both of the operative zones, North-West and South-East Herzegovina; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection about the way the concept "Muslim men" was used here. The order makes this perfectly clear. These are HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, and Muslims of military age. I think to generalise like this is entirely erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I believe the question is a fair question. I think the documents and the evidence that we're going to go through don't distinguish between Muslims who are members of the HVO and Muslim men of military age who were civilians. All were arrested, without distinction. That's our position, and that's what I'm going to be putting to the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, getting back -- well, let me just read, to bring us back to your testimony from before, on the 25th of August. I said: "At the time you took command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, General Petkovic didn't tell you about any of that?" I'm asking you about an order to remove Muslims who had been members of the HVO and disarmament. And you said: "No, we did not have any time to talk about that."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's look at the first document on this, which is P03019. Before we do, let me ask you, though, General, about the period after the 24th of July, 1993. After the 24th of July, were Muslim members of the HVO disarmed and imprisoned based on your orders or based on a continuation of an order issued by General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue an order like that. I am not aware of any such incident later on. I didn't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if the HVO was arresting Muslim -- if the HVO was arresting Muslim members of the HVO and putting them in prison after the 24th of July, you're telling us you didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if the HVO was arresting Muslim men between the ages of 16 and 60, even if they were not members of the HVO, were you aware that that was taking place after the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you didn't know it at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The first document is P03019. This is dated the 30th of June, 1993, and this is General Petkovic, in item 8, paragraph 8: "As chief of the HVO Main Staff, orders that in units where you still have Muslim soldiers, disarm and isolate them. Isolate all able-bodied men in Muslim-inhabited villages in your area of responsibility and leave women and children in their houses and apartments." So, General, you're telling us that you were not aware of this order on or about the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I would like to set the record straight. He is not saying that Muslim soldiers should be arrested, but rather Bojovnici, which means HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, that they should be disarmed and isolated. All able-bodied men shall be isolated, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, actually, one could interpret this as addressing three categories of people, couldn't it? The first category being Muslims who were members of the HVO, they have to be disarmed and isolated; and then, secondly, another category would be all able-bodied men in Muslim-inhabited villages should be isolated; and then the third category would be the women and children who should be left in their houses and apartments. But we'll leave that for another day, in terms of the interpretation, because we recognise you didn't write this order, General. I'm asking you: You didn't know about it on the 30th of June or in the days and weeks that followed the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in Boksevica, and later I left for Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, again, General Petkovic never brought this order or this to your attention at the time he handed over the command to you on the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problems we were facing on the 24th of July were far too great for us to be dealing with something that had occurred twenty-four days earlier. We were facing far too great problems in order to avoid losing everything after Bugojno all the way up to the western borders based on Sefer Halilovic's plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if the HVO was isolating and detaining Muslim men throughout the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, that wasn't something that was important enough to get on your radar screen when you took command; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm telling you the problems we were facing on the 24th were so great that an order like this warranted not much attention or time. There was no need to discuss it. Anyway, it is my personal view that if that's what you're trying to say, from a military perspective, I think General Petkovic's order is perfectly fair following the treason and everything else that happened in Eastern Herzegovina Operative Zone, everything that the Muslims within the HVO did there. That is what the military rules dictate you must do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we're going to talk about the places where all these people were detained later in the next binder. But, General, then given the fact that this is a large number of people who are going to be isolated and detained, doesn't this raise a very important issue for you, as commander of the HVO Main Staff, in respect of the detention facilities and the treatment of all of these people who are being detained on the orders of General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm telling you I didn't know. And then you go telling me, Okay, so then you knew, so well then -- and then I'm telling you again I didn't know. And then again your next question has no -- I was not aware of the development or, indeed, the numbers of men involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, based on what you learned later, it's true, isn't it, that when General Petkovic handed over the command of the Main Staff to you, he also handed over to you thousands of Muslim prisoners, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. It contains the presumption that the prisoners were under the jurisdiction of the chief of the Main Staff, about which we have not seen a single shred of evidence in this courtroom that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the last part of Ms. Alaburic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please repeat the last part of your -- what you said, because it was not recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is about the presumption contained in my learned friend Mr. Stringer's question to the effect that General Petkovic, as chief of the Main Staff, had some powers over thousands of Muslim prisoners and could, therefore, go to General Praljak, as the new commander of the HVO Main Staff, those prisoners. Therefore, this presumed fact has not been backed by a single shred of evidence during this trial so far. That is why I believe the question to be irregular. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll deal with this issue during the course of the cross-examination. Needless to say the Prosecution position is that when prisoners are arrested on the orders of the military commander, he can't just pass off responsibility for them to others without ensuring that his responsibilities are being discharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may say, if I may, I believe it a valuable thing that the OTP should put forward their position, but may I please be allowed to present our Defence position? There is a difference between isolating a person and imprisoning a person. There is also a difference between that and monitoring the prisons. Powers over these activities can be attributed to various state authorities or organs in this case of Herceg-Bosna. The presumption expressed by the OTP is, therefore, neither logical nor, indeed, well founded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This had not escaped me. I had intended to ask a question on this, on this word "izolirati" in Croatian. I will deal with this later on when Mr. Stringer is done with the document. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. What I would like to do is move to the next document and then perhaps suggest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before then, General Praljak, I would like to study this order by General Petkovic. It's not yours; we know that. We know it was General Petkovic's order, but I have a question, a linguistic question first. In your own language, when you start a sentence by the letter U, at point 5, "U," and so forth, what does this mean, this "U"? What does it mean, this "U"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that those people in the units, so an HVO in that area comprises Croats and Muslims. They are in those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier, the Prosecutor told you of three situations, starting with paragraph 8, and I see a fourth situation that was not mentioned by Mr. Stringer. The first situation is that of Muslim members of the HVO; they are to be disarmed and isolated. The second situation, able-bodied men -- able-bodied Muslim men, they are also supposed to be isolated. And then children and women that are supposed to stay home. But what about a fourth category; older Muslim men over 60 years old, or 70 or 80 - I don't know what the age limit was - those who cannot be mobilised, these older people, what is their fate? Are they supposed to be arrested also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's why it reads "all able-bodied men." In military-speak, "able-bodied men" are those who are potential military conscripts, who fall under an obligation to do military service. So if they are not able-bodied in relation to the army, that would imply that they are either women or children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now come to Ms. Alaburic's objection. You know, when I have a document in front of me, I look at it from beginning to end. Maybe this is why I spend a lot of time putting questions later on. But it did strike me that we did have this word "isolated." They are not detained; they're isolated. So I was wondering why this term "izolirati" was used. Is this just used as any other word, or does this have a very specific legal meaning? So in Croatian, when someone uses this word, "izolirati," what exactly does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, and that is strictly my interpretation, it means to make it impossible for them to move, to move about. People are placed in a certain place or left back in their own homes, and one makes sure they can't move around. For example, after what happened in Uzdol, I isolated the Muslim religious official from the area in order to prevent any acts of retaliation and keeping from getting himself killed, so I isolated him. Even when you have large gatherings of statesmen, they have to be isolated, and these statesmen, when meeting at the highest possible level, are not allowed to move around anywhere they like. It's a security issue, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. I always look at the dates on documents because I believe that context is essential. You absolutely have to place a document back into the context, because otherwise you might run into misunderstandings. So could you please tell us what had happened prior to June 30th regarding Muslim units of the HVO, either prior to that date or on that date, and could you be very specific so this is recorded on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The summary would be as follows: Let us assume that we here are a single army and we have weapons. On the 30th of June, I turn my weapon on you, honourable Judge Antonetti, be it in order to arrest you, or in order to kill you, or in order to take you to prison. I take over control over the lines in their entirety, and that's what the HVO soldiers did on the 30th of June in the broader Mostar area, facing their erstwhile fellows, Croat fighters. This is an act of treason, and in any normal army these people would have been shot on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's something wrong with the interpretation or the transcript, or maybe the general misspoke. Can he please repeat this key sentence. What happened on the 30th of June? Which soldiers did what on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity or, rather -- or, well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, throughout the conflict, as you told us often, the problem of troops was important to you, was a shortage of troops, so it was very important. You know, able-bodied men were important. When you took over command of the HVO, did you ever compare your -- the number of troops you had with what you had before, maybe? Did you ever say, Well, at first I had so many troops and now I only have this many left? So did you ever make a comparison between the numbers of troops you had at one point in time with what you had before? Did you ever check whether there was any attrition in the number of fighters? And here I'm thinking about the Muslim members of the HVO. And did you ever look into their fate, what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment, no. Right there and then, I had to be off to Gornji Vakuf. You did see the document, about 15 days later on, when I demanded that the exact number of soldiers be ascertained, not based on any lists that were blown out of all proportion for all sorts of reasons, but rather the real number of men who were prepared to fight. The discrepancy between the lists that were being floated around and the actual number was quite considerable. In my own area, as you've seen already, I made my own estimate with those words at the end, and I'm not repeating those words, the words expressing some sort of resignation, desperation, if you like, desperation at the miserably small number of splintered units. They were great, they did a great job fighting, but it was difficult to have such a small number of units, between 20 and 100 people, and defend such a broad front in Gornji Vakuf. It was then that I started to realise what the actual number of men were who were prepared to go to the front-lines and not those who were just trying to escape, who were hiding somewhere, who were wounded, who had lost the mental ability to fight, so on and -- or the physical ability, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the end of the translation. So you never tried to find out where those missing soldiers had gone or what had become of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never wondered, to be quite frank. I hadn't found out before the 1st of September, obviously, that there was a problem, to begin with. When Ms. Ivanisevic came, I gave her a pass. I keep saying this. If we forget the amount of aggression being carried out by the BH Army at this point in time, then it's very difficult to understand what a certain person did. All these questions are very neat, but I never got as far as asking myself these questions. I had to evacuate the wounded, the wounded of the BH Army from Mostar, and then arming Central Bosnia by helicopters, Zepce, evacuating the wounded, and I don't know if anybody at all can understand the amount of problems being faced by a commander facing such aggression, with as many men available to him as were available to me, and trying to keep myself from getting defeated, and that was my principle task. Let's not forget about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, just looking at the last part of your answer to Judge Mindua's question here, where you're talking about the many things that you were involved in, evacuating wounded, wounded of the BH Army from Mostar, arming Central Bosnia by helicopters, Zepce, evacuating the wounded, I mean, the fact is that you're involved in a tremendous number of things at the same time when you claim to have no knowledge of the detention or the isolation of thousands of Muslim men right in your own back yard. Now, that's not believable, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to you. To me, it is perfectly believable. These were my military commitments. It is a very important thing that a wounded person, or soldier, should be seen to. That is an obligation for me, a military one. If this person remains alive, they have to be seen to. And the same thing applied to the four groups of wounded of the BH Army who were evacuated. What you appear to be thinking, that I had the time to do this or that, or I didn't have the time to do this or that, I fought in the hills of Mostar, in the north, in the south, and during the lulls there were the military problems that had to do with organising for the survival of Tihomir Blaskic's operative zone, the survival of Zepce, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In order to look after the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Zepce, which was quite a distance removed from your own location, you had to be well informed of the events in all of those areas, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What events? That they were running out of ammunition, that the BH Army was attacking them, that I was supposed to violate the weapons embargo, yes, that was the kind of information, in addition to everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You had to know the situation on the ground in all of those areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
