utterances.text: The military situation, yes. What exactly do you mean when you say "know the situation"? The military situation, I knew the military situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then maybe that's why we're not -- we're not together. Let me put this to you: It seems to me, sir, that what you're suggesting is that in respect of Muslim prisoners or detainees, people isolated, that did not fall within one of your military commitments.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that didn't come within my military commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you neither -- you neither knew about them, and even if you did know about them, they did not fall within your responsibility; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that. But you could say that even if I did know, if a prisoner had been handed over, he is no longer the responsibility of the Main Staff. Prisons did not come under the authority of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The prisons came under the authority -- well, let's be clear what we're talking about. When you say "prisons," what prisons do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say which prisons I had in mind. I didn't know which prisons existed, except that I knew that there was the prison at Heliodrom, and I did know that there was a prison in Dretelj. I did in September, but I thought it was a prison and it was a prison, and I asked that they -- that those members of the HVO who had committed infractions, not crimes but infractions, should be put there, so misdemeanors, et cetera. And I think you saw that in the documents, which on the 25th or 20th of September, I issued. And as far as I was concerned, that was a prison, and I asked that everybody be put in one place. So those members of the HVO who had been punished by a commander because of infractions of some kind, they were sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I do -- yes, I do remember that exhibit, General. In respect of Muslim prisoners or detainees held at Dretelj, if you're claiming they were not the responsibility of the Main Staff, are you saying that they were the responsibility of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, the fact that the prisons did not come under the responsibility of the Main Staff in any way during the time that I was down there, and that's a fact, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question is this: If they did not fall under your responsibility, did they fall under the responsibility of the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What about the military police? Were they the responsibility of the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You had a man here from the other legal area, so you could have cleared that up with him. I'm not an expert in the area, nor was it in my job description as commander of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council during the material time when I performed that duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. You mentioned your job description, Mr. Praljak. Could you produce a copy of your job description? If yes, then I would be pleased to see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, all documents on establishment for the HVO have already been shown here, and they've been given a number and were admitted, and it says precisely who did what in the HVO, whether in the civilian or the military section. They're already an exhibit, as far as I remember, in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I then -- I will try, then, to get it and to read it, and I will also check what you claimed, that there was nothing written about those issues which we talked about it during the last couple of minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I've already asked you questions regarding those prisoners, and you had replied by saying they did not fall under your responsibility, and you have mentioned this again to the Prosecutor. I will look at it from another point of view or from another angle. You are the HVO commander, and during some fights it could be that some prisoners were taken. Yesterday, we saw that 23 HVO soldiers were detained or were held prisoner - we saw that yesterday - in Gornji Vakuf. We also know that the ABiH was detaining HVO prisoners. We're also aware that the HVO was also holding some military prisoners from the ABiH. And through the evidence, we know that there was an office in charge of prisoner exchanges. These are facts that we have before us. Based on all this, as a commander, the fact that you have prisoners could come into play regarding the morale of the troops, and in fact I saw this morning that you're going to have an expert who is going to talk about psychological problems that could have some consequences on soldiers. This will be interesting, and I suppose that we're going to touch on these issues again. But as HVO commander, you know that there are some soldiers that are held by the enemy, and you know that exchanges can be made. I was wondering whether you were not dealing at all with this aspect of things. I've already asked this question and you've already answered, but I insist on this, once again, because as part of your duties as commander, this was something to take into account, the morale of the troops. And if you knew that amongst the soldiers maybe some had a father or a brother that was detained by the enemy, it plays on the morale of the troops. And you seem to say that you were not dealing at all with this, so what is your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem of exchanges is quite another matter, and I couldn't deal with that either at the time, although it's an important issue. Unfortunately, I was not able to deal with that type of thing, but I did know that at the level of the HVO there were daily negotiations underway on the exchange of prisoners and that Mr. Pusic, whom I had heard was doing this kind of job, was doing it well. Now, the wounded, the BH Army wounded, well, at the time I was involved in an agreement for boosting morale, that we would enable all wounded BH Army soldiers to be pulled out from Mostar, from East Mostar, and that they would enable us to have reciprocal treatment. Unfortunately, I agreed four times, to do that kind of thing four times, whereas they withheld their reciprocity, and then some people ambushed the helicopters that we talked about because they expected if we comply, that they would comply and that their sons would be returned. So these were rebellious people who took the helicopters. And I wouldn't have avoided that problem, given the time, but as I say, it was a very difficult situation during the war, and if we gave way, we would become involved in other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Praljak, I would like to ask questions on this topic. As you have noticed, the topic of prisoners is very important. You said that HVO Muslim soldiers who turn their weapons against their brothers of the HVO should be set aside. And you added that, generally speaking, soldiers of that kind are executed or shot. And I believe you're right, it is the case in a lot of armies. This is the situation that is provided for in a lot of military laws. I would like to come back to the question that I asked before regarding the number of troops or what we talk -- what we call military establishment plans. Every morning we check on troops, and I'm sure that it is even more important in a wartime setting. Following this order, when we are asking to set aside soldiers or to isolate soldiers that are subject to treason, a commander who is in charge takes into account the morale of the troops. They make sure that they eat well, and so on and so forth. A commander who likes his troops and who sees that some have been traitors and could be shot on the spot, and this is what you said, once those soldiers have been separated from the group, a commander who usually likes his troops is no longer interested. So what I was wondering is as soon as a soldier has come out of the ranks, that's it, you do no longer care whether they are shot on the spot, executed, sent to prison, given to animals? You do not care; is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, as far as I know, is when -- well, what happens next is not up to the commander. He has to do two things; to isolate the people, not to carry on with the damage they've done and, secondly, isolation is put in force so that retaliation should not be against them, because they might have killed their colleagues or whatever. So retaliation and revenge is a very real possibility, and you have to isolate the people to avoid that from happening. And then the military police takes over, and military police procedure, and then the commander no longer has -- at least as far as I know and as far as I'm concerned, and I do know about this, there are the court organs that raise an indictment, that investigate, that launch an inquiry, and everything else that is customary in other armies as well. If I've answered your question, so an HVO soldier hands over a prisoner to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood very well, Witness Praljak. I was waiting for the end of the interpretation. So according to what you're saying, as soon as the soldiers were no longer part of the troops, that was it, you were forgetting about them fully. That's very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to try to expand this just a little bit to make sure we understand precisely your position. We've been talking about, well, different categories, and going back to the order that we looked at from General Petkovic, the Muslims who were members of the HVO and who were disarmed and who were placed in isolation, let's say that they are -- they are isolated at Dretelj. Now, is it your position that those individuals are not part of the responsibility of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, another category was Muslim men, able-bodied, not members of the HVO, but who are detained and isolated. Are those individuals also not part of the responsibility of the Main Staff, in your view?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were incarcerated after that, they are not. If they are isolated, then one day that isolation period will cease when the danger passes for which they are placed in isolation in the first place. But you'll have General Petkovic, so he can tell you about that. But all this is -- the hypotheses are quite in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about something maybe that you know more about. You've been telling us about the ABiH offensive that took place in -- after you became commander of the HVO Main Staff, and that you were up fighting in Gornji Vakuf and the Prozor area; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the offensive didn't take place after I came -- became commander of the Main Staff. It came about much earlier, starting from Konjic, which ended as it ended, and especially Bugojno, which was well before I arrived, and I had to confront the situation of 1.500 -- 2.000 soldiers and a large force of the BH Army launching itself on Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's say that in August of 1993, in Gornji Vakuf, the HVO captures some ABiH soldiers, who then become prisoners of war. Are those prisoners of war then under the responsibility of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the Main Staff, in your view, has not -- has no responsibilities in respect of any of those -- those prisoners that we've been talking about. Are there any prisoners of the HVO that the Main Staff does have responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoners of the HVO, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are there any prisoners of the HVO for which the Main Staff is responsible?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, I don't understand what this means, prisoners of the HVO. What? Yes, yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me try to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer, I'll answer, I'll answer. The HVO -- well, soldiers who would capture enemy soldiers are responsible for that prisoner until they hand him over to the military police. At that point in time, that very moment, their responsibility ceases, as far as prisoners are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So any prisoners handed over to the military police then, it then it becomes the responsibility of the military police to ensure that those prisoners are treated properly? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. That's another aspect, and you had people dealing with legal issues here. Now, what happened next? What happens afterwards? Who interviews them? Who appoints commanders, wardens of prisons or whatever? You had other people to ask those questions about. And you're asking me this, but I don't want to speculate. A soldier is handed over to the military police. What the procedure is after that, I don't know, and I don't want to speculate. No matter how much you try to make me do so, you're not going to succeed in that, Mr. Stringer. We're here to establish the following: that an HVO soldier is duty-bound to hand over a prisoner to the military police. That's his duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you said to the Prosecutor that there are some areas where you do not want to answer. I would like to remind you, General Praljak, that you said that you wanted to testify and tell the truth. And the Rules and Regulations say that you cannot answer a question if you feel that they are incriminating questions. The Rules are very well drafted, because they do not take into account the fact that an accused witness is always border-line and that at the end of the day he or she could be led to answer incriminating questions, but you have the possibility to say to the Prosecutor, I do not want to answer this question because I feel that this question is incriminating. And there is nothing that we can do, even if the Rules say that we can ask you to answer, but we give you immunity, which would be paradoxical, which is why there is a slight flaw in the Regulations in the Rules. Whatever the case may be, the Prosecutor is asking you questions on prisoners, and it's not a new question because I asked you this question as well. And you say, It is not my responsibility, and you stop here. Why are you now saying to Mr. Stringer that you do no longer want to answer this question? This is what I don't understand. So perhaps there is a mistake in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say I did not want to answer. I said I don't want to speculate. I don't want to rattle on about things that I don't know about; who appoints a warden, who provides security, who replaces whom, who examines and questions, who raises an indictment. I know something about those things, but my knowledge is insufficient for me to be able to hold forth here. So it's not that I don't want to answer. I don't know about these things well enough. And you had prison wardens, you had military policemen who were witnesses, you had legal experts, without Praljak, you discussed these issues without Praljak, and now you expect me to talk about these things. But when I don't know something, I say, I don't know. My lack of knowledge is vast, but my knowledge is also vast. So I give precise answers where I can. When I'm asked to speculate and talk about things I'm not sure about, I don't wish to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand correctly, you said you were prepared to answer questions, all questions that will be asked, but there are some areas that go beyond your skills or your competence, and you have named a few, such as those appointing prison wardens and so on. Mr. Stringer is going to take that into account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps take a break now? I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document in the binder is P03026, 3026. General, this is a communication from Colonel Siljeg to the Defence Department, attention Bruno Stojic, and also to the Main Staff, attention Major Milivoj Petkovic, 30th of June. And just for the record, General, the 30th of June being the date of the ABiH attack on the Southern Barracks in the Mostar area. And what Siljeg says at the beginning of this, is he says: "Brada was familiarised with the report from Mostar, with the conversation between Pasalic and Halilovic and with the command issued by the head of the Defence Department and the president of the HVO HZ-HB." General, just before we go any farther, would you agree with me if I suggested to you that the Brada who Siljeg is referring to here is you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was at Boksevica, and I don't know -- I've read this document. How could I have known about these orders and what this was about, for me to give instructions from Boksevica? I don't think that could be correct, because I know exactly what I was doing on the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you, General, that in fact this is a reference to you and that you were in communication with Siljeg, as he's indicated here, and that based on his conversation with you, Siljeg did issue -- or that Siljeg did make these three requests that are indicated. So, General, my question is, though you probably already answered it: On the 30th of June, you were in communication with Siljeg, and you were briefed on the events that had occurred on that day, at least, about the ABiH attack and the command issued by Mr. Stojic and Prlic that's referred to here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, sir. I repeat, if someone wants me to, I can describe exactly what the fighting on Dreznica looked like. I would not like to confirm that this was about me issuing instructions of this type. That is simply not possible. I was just a fighter over there, and you will see people say that. A man will appear here to testify about that, so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is that there's no other Brada who would -- who Siljeg would be conferring with about these very important topics on the 30th of June; isn't that true? The only Brada he could be referring to is you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is another reference to another name -- to another man named Brada. I don't know who that was in reference to. Again, I find it entirely unclear that I might be issuing instructions to Obradovic to take Blagaj, and to Petkovic as to what he should do in the situation as it was. This is nonsense. I'm looking at this report by Mr. Siljeg, and I have to say I don't think it was created based on a conversation that he actually had with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to the next exhibit, then, P03234. Now, General, this is another document from Siljeg. This one's dated the 6th of July, 1993, and he orders that: "In accordance with the current situation in the area of Rama-Prozor municipality, I hereby order: "Arrest and detain all Muslim men aged between 16 and 60. "The following are responsible for the carrying out of this order: the military police and the SIS of the Rama Brigade." Now, General, this is the 6th of July. I know, or you've indicated you were in Boksevica at the time. Did you become aware of this order at any time on or after the 6th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, then, is P03380. Now, this is the 11th of July, and this is a report from Luka Markesic. And it says: "On the basis of the order of the commander of the 2nd Operative Zone number 1489/93, dated 6 July ..." And by the reference numbers, General, we know that that's a reference to the Siljeg order that we just looked at: " ... and further instructions of the above-named officer, the following persons of Muslim nationality are to be sent to the Ljubuski Military Prison." They are to be sent to the Ljubuski Military Prison. And then this has a list. And, General, I've learned that the translation -- this is the translation we have in e-court, but it's not -- it's clearly not a complete one, and so I want to ask you if you can just tell us some things based upon your reading of the original language version just so that we can get that on the record and get this translation fixed, because on the last page of the English you'll see that Markesic says: "We hereby inform you that 237 members of Muslim nationality (military conscripts) have been sent from Rama-Prozor, escorted by military police." So now, General, looking at the original language version of this, just to make sure we've got it correct, this is a list of 237 Muslim prisoners, or persons, I should say, who are being sent to Ljubuski Military Prison. Isn't that what's indicated here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the translation of the previous one at all, no translation. I have a list, but no translation of the Luka Markesic document, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I see that you're looking at the document I'm looking at. Let's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So -- and if you turn to the third page of that, then, you'll see that it ends with number 237.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the text that follows after the person whose name is typed there as number 237, I don't know that that text, Mr. President, found its way into the translation, so I'd like to ask the general to read that out loud for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, can you read the text that follows after number 237?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We hereby note that the persons listed above are no POWs; rather, these are persons who have been detained for security reasons. The persons listed above will be escorted by the following military policemen." And then a list of nine persons that follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then just to complete this, could you read the passage that follows, that ends with the number 9.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list ends with number 9: "On behalf of the Security Service, Luka Markesic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then, General, would you agree with me that what appears next to that is a stamp of the HVO Main Staff, dated the 11th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an incoming stamp, but there is no Main Staff stamp. He dispatched this to the SIS Mostar Administration and the operative zone SIS. That's as much as I can tell from looking at page 1. I don't know why this document would be received by the Main Staff. It was never dispatched to the Main Staff, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But, in fact, the stamp tells us that for some reason it was received at the Main Staff on the 11th of July, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, whether it was received or not or why, indeed, the information is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to draw the Chamber's attention, and I think we have been tendering evidence about that as well, there will be more about that later on, the incoming stamp on the last page of the original shows no more than this: The document was processed through a packet communications system belonging to the Main Staff, and then we have a different book, another book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think there's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise to interrupt, Mr. President, but I think we'd object to counsel making arguments about what the document does or doesn't show. That's for a later time. And what the witness has just said is that it's an incoming stamp at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you are making us waste time because this question has already been touched upon by you or your colleagues. I can remember this. I do not have the transcripts, but I have quite a good memory. You have all said that the receiving stamp means a certain thing; namely, that it is registered where the stamp arrived -- where the document arrives, but it doesn't mean that the HVO commander, or number 1, or number 2, or number 3, were made aware of this. So you've said that before. So if it reaches the Main Staff, we do not know where it goes thereafter, and we assume that it has arrived at the Main Staff. That's all. So you've already said it, so why say it again, Mr. Kovacic? We are not stupid. You know full well that Judges follow this very closely, second by second, everything that is being said, everything that is put to us. So what you said, it has already been taken on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That wasn't the gist. I know you know that; I know we've spoken about that. It was just by way of introduction that I was trying to explain about this, the point being, though, the Prosecutor cannot show a document and put it to a witness that this was received at the Main Staff. It wasn't. It's precisely what you were saying now and what we know. This merely confirms that it was received by the communications hub, the communications centre. My only objection is about this: When a question is being asked, one cannot be putting things to a witness that don't follow from the document being presented. But it's done and dusted now, unfortunately, now, so now that I'm taking up your time, the translation of this document, you see you've got in your binder, there are two translations of two documents. The first consistent with the original, consistent only up to 216, number 216 of the list, and there is nothing further there. The translation is entirely incomplete. I assume that was why my learned friend asked the witness to -- and then there's another translation, a two-page document, with no original attached. It appears to have ended up here by mistake, or at least that's what I assume. Perhaps it might be a good idea for the OTP to attach a full translation, because this one is marked as a draft translation, a full translation, pages 1 to 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you said is on the transcript. As Judge Mindua said, most Judges did their national service, so they know all this. You know, they did their military service. I, myself, was in the Transmission Department when I was in my military -- when I was doing my military service, so I was filling in these kind of documents. You know, I know exactly all this. And we all know that it's not because some NCO is going to fill in the case and so that this rectangle, you know, that everyone will know at the chain of command. You've said this over and over again. Okay, you want this on the transcript, well, it is noted on the transcript now, but we already knew it. Now, as far as translation was concerned, I believe Mr. Stringer had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well just to inform the Chamber and everyone, we looked into this, there was an earlier translation that did not contain all of the names of the Muslim arrestees. And then, of course, we have this translation, which is the one in e-court, which we work with. It's our impression -- I'm not sure, but this might be one of the documents where the Trial Chamber asked that it be fully translated to include all of the names of the prisoners, because there have been times when the Trial Chamber has asked to get all the names listed. So we think that the translation was sent across to be modified and then it just ended up being the way it is, which is incomplete. So it's -- if I could just finish, and then I'll yield to my learned friend. We just discovered this the other day. It's in e-court, and so we can't change it. And so my way of dealing with it was to bring it to everyone's attention and to ask the witness to address the parts that are not found in the translation while we get the translation corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one observation, with your leave. This appears, in my respectful submission, to be an example of a lack of adherence to the most basic of procedural rules, opening up a hornet's nest, because when one party -- I know there was a comment from the Chamber. When one party in effect gives evidence, of course it leaves the door wide open for other parties to do that. And in the end all that happens is that a considerable amount of court time is wasted. And I would urge, Your Honours, that all parties exercise discipline in separating testimony from the Bar table to questions which -- and objections which, of course, are matters that can be raised in court. Evidence should be led in the normal manner, not be given by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Let's try and save some time. Notably, when a counsel is addressing a question that has already been mentioned, if it's new, fine, but if -- you just tell us. But if you're revisiting an issue, please refrain from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want to say that I'm not aware that we -- and no one has said the Chamber -- a member of the Chamber, as has been said, asked for all the names to be copied, because that's not translation, that's copying. And we have numerous lists from all sides in this Chamber where we had long lists of names, and we had the first and the last names, and then it was said we have so many in between, and that's exactly what we have in the first translation. So I think the second one is really made for the waste paper basket and of no use at all, and the first one is completely satisfactory, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is exactly the case. I agree 100 per cent. The only problem is that the first one finishes with number 216 and with no -- with no two sentences which are in original -- so basically now we have all the translation in two documents, still without some persons listed, which is not important. But we have to go in two documents to see the translation. It's complicated. But I think there is no need to discuss that. The Prosecution clearly said that they will -- that they will submit complete translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to avoid misunderstandings, what you refer to as the first document in my binder is the second one, and I think that it is completely enough to have the document which has the first name, then says so-and-so many other names, and the last name, and then all the rest is complete. So it's the one you have referred to with the 216 names that I think is for the waste paper basket, or the shredder, if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following what my fellow Judge Trechsel just said, I believe that Mr. Stringer has an excellent memory. I'm not really sure that this is the document in question, but I know that there was a document where the Trial Chamber asked for the translation of the names who were on the list. I can't really remember what the reason was for this, and Mr. Stringer reminded us of this, and that's it. So unless he suddenly is suffering from memory loss, I think that's what he said, and that's why he said it. But our legal officer will make some research. But I think it was a request by Judge Trechsel to have for this translation. That's all I remember about this at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... react with the last words -- with the last words of "Some Like It Hot;" namely, nobody's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the record and because of the comment made by Judge Trechsel, the translation of this document is -- P00380, the document we're discussing, does not have all the names, but just the first and last sentence. This is incomplete; it's an incomplete translation of the document. Therefore, the document must be read along with the transcript, when General Praljak read into the transcript the missing sentences, the sentences saying about these person lists, that these were no POWs, but rather these persons were detained for security reasons. Detained, yes, that's what it says. Therefore, that portion, too, should be included in the final translation of the document. Once you get down to analysing this document, you need to have the full text in front of you, and that's why our proposal was, in e-court, with the Court's leave, to have there a new translation and a full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate on this, because I believe there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just make one -- I apologise. The Prosecution agrees with the comments of Ms. Pinter. The sentence that we asked the general to read about the distinction between prisoners of war and people being detained for security reasons we think is a significant one, and it doesn't appear in the translation that is in e-court. And so it's a CLSS translation which the OTP cannot fix. It's in e-court, so the OTP can't change what's in e-court, and so we would join in the suggestion of Ms. Pinter that the original language version of this document be resubmitted to CLSS to make sure that it is full and complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will deliberate on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated on this and notes that both parties believe that it's necessary for the document to be fully translated, and is thus -- the Trial Chamber is thus asking the CLSS to translate the document in full. And the Trial Chamber will then ask the OTP to download this newly-translated document into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just a last question, getting back to this document we've been talking about. This is the 11th of July, 1993, which I understand it is just about the time that you left from Boksevica and headed back out to Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 11th of July, I was in Zagreb then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that. So I take it, then, that these 237 Muslim people who were to be sent to the Ljubuski Prison, you didn't know about this at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know. Now, as to whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm looking at your testimony from the 26th of May, and you were talking about Boksevica, and you said -- that's page 40777, line 11: "I spent 11 or 12 days there until the 9th of July, 1993." And then you talk about the situation there in Boksevica. And then I'm turning the page to the next page of the transcript. You say -- you say: "It was impossible to hold Boksevica any longer, and we'll abandon those positions there, too." And then you said: "Then I went to see Mate Boban. I discussed the whole situation with him. I think I had a brief meeting with Mr. Petkovic, or, rather, that's not what I think; I know that we met. We talked a while, as normal people." And I'm going to skip down a couple lines. And then you said: "And in the evening -- well, I spoke to Mr. Stojic, and in the evening, I believe it was the 10th or something like that, the 10th of May -- sorry, the 10th of July, 1993, I came to his place to take a bath and to eat something because the food up there, well, there was nothing up there." And then I'm skipping down. You say: "I took a bath, and the next morning I went to Zagreb for private reasons, because my father was very ill." Now, that would indicate, General, that as you've indicated, on the 11th of July, you left for Zagreb. My question is this: In your discussions, your meetings, the time you spent with Mr. Boban, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Stojic, in Mostar on the 9th or 10th of July, did they inform you at all about the arrests and the isolation of Muslim men that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I informed them about Boksevica alone, not the other way around. I told them what had happened, how many people were pulled out, and precisely the way I said it, although you could put everything forward by a day. Those were very brief talks with Mate Boban, not more than ten minutes, because he thought that we could still hold control of Boksevica. I refuted that and was angry because I knew exactly what was happening up there. Now, with Mr. Stojic, I think I finished with him that very same evening. I stank like a skunk, so I had a bath. I was hungry and thirsty. It's cold on the mountain. And then I went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you would turn -- I'm going to skip one document, General, and ask you to go to P03455. This is from the 14th of July, 1993. And recognising that you were in Zagreb at the time, this is a communication from General Petkovic to Colonel Siljeg, and it's about a number of different topics. I'm interested in item number 12, where Petkovic says: "I have given you permission for the Muslims. Transfer them from the area." And then let me just --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's item number 12.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a very poor copy. I can't read it. I can't read those two lines or part of a line, so I don't actually know what it says here exactly because my copy is a very poor one; it's illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Possibly if the Registrar could take that part and make it bigger or blow it up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've read item 11 now. You mean item 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, item 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then we'll come back to it, but let's first look at the next document, which is P03498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, are you going to come back to this document; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm going to link this document to the next one, which is P03498, or I'm going to try to link it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is 16 July 1993, so it's two days after the preceding -- the communication from Petkovic to Siljeg. And this is a report of, again, Luka Markesic, and here he's listing 155 persons of Muslim nationality who are being sent to military prison, and this is on the basis of the 6th of July order that we looked at a little while ago from Colonel Siljeg. So two days after the communication from General Petkovic, then we see these individuals being sent. General, the question is now, because we're getting close -- this is just eight days before you take command of the HVO Main Staff, and, General, I'm going to challenge you. The fact is, General, that you did know about all of these Muslim people who were being sent off to military prison from the Prozor area. You learned about it when you came back and took command of the HVO Main Staff. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So Siljeg then -- not only General Petkovic, but Colonel Siljeg never told you about these Muslims who were being sent to the military prisons, then, throughout the time that you were in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit -- I apologise, Mr. President. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a marginal detail because, you know, I scrutinize these documents. Of course, I listened to the Prosecution's case, but I also try to take on board other angles. There's 155 detained -- 135 detained people, prisoners, who are sent to the prison. We have a list, and at the very end of the document I see that these people are going to be escorted with two -- there are two names being listed, but there's only one military policeman, Marko Bosnjak. Given this, we have 155 prisoners escorted with only one single military policeman, or maybe two at the most. This seems to show that the mindset of these prisoners was such that they were not much of a security issue, they weren't going to escape or anything, obviously. Of course, General Praljak, you have no elements at hand - at least that's what you're saying. But I'm looking at things from another angle. When you have 155 prisoners escorted by only one or two policemen, military policemen, what does this mean? What can this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I might be allowed to speculate. What this is about here is that they are being transferred for security reasons, if I understand this correctly, so security reasons and considerations. And can I expand and say I think you saw a document of mine from October, when the situation was calm around Uzdol and when there was no retaliation, and then the offensive started. But for security reasons I issued an order on that particular occasion to put the Muslims in one place. Now, when you understand that you cannot protect some people from retaliation, 15.000 refugees, and soldiers and so on, perhaps it would be logical to move these people to another place, because you cannot ensure their security, so you have to choose. You always have to choose between the bad and the even worse. It's bad to transfer people, but it's even worse if you're powerless to protect them from somebody retaliating, somebody being killed, raped, or whatever. So you have to choose between a rock and a hard place, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, the fact is that if you're interested in looking after the security of the Muslim population, you would have moved all of them, not just the men of military age; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you're making me guess, or you're guessing. When I transferred people for some reason, I transferred everyone, so don't move into the realm of over-speculation. I can tell you what I did and why, and if you want to ask me more, then I'll give you a precise answer, The reason for my decision was such and such. I'll be able to do that for each of my decisions, if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the fact that in these documents we're looking at, where only Muslim men of military age are being moved, that tells us that this is not about doing it for their own security, but rather this is a security measure done to protect the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking me to guess, to speculate about a document compiled by one person, implemented by another, and so on and so forth. I think you're asking me too much. I don't suppose you want me to guess and speculate and so on, because I have already been asked questions which range from history to all manner of areas, but I don't know what you want me to do. I was in Zagreb, so who thought what and how you could interpret what, I leave that to the Judges. They're here to interpret and to decide. I can tell you about my documents, and what I took a part in, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, your reaction is a bit surprising, because a short while ago you have told us that this was done for the security of these people. Now, the Prosecutor puts it to you that it's not very convincing. Would you say that you also speculated before, or would you make a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was guessing. I said, Hypothetically, perhaps, maybe, if that was recorded in the translation, the interpretation. I was asked to say something, Judge Antonetti, and I speculate, I put forward a theory, I say, Maybe, possibly. That's what it should have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 56, line 17 -- or the word appears in line 18 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you want to lead me on from one set of speculations to another, to a third, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this context, might I be allowed to say that on page 57, line 13, it was clearly recorded that General Praljak was talking about transferring people from those areas and not the fact of their isolation. So then those two actions, I think Mr. Stringer mixed them up, and I think it was between isolation and transference. And that's why I think Judge Trechsel misunderstood General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was answering a precise question from Judge Antonetti, precisely, as a possibility, as a hypothetical. Now, on the basis of one possibility, to turn it into a fact and conclusion, that is simply not in order, logically speaking, and I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, General. The next exhibit is a video-clip. It's from the interview that you gave to the BBC. It's not in the binder. We've looked at a few of these already. This is P09258, and hopefully the technology will not fail us this time, and we can listen to this part of your interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The second question is about detention centres. On the 17th of July, 1993, the news about the existence of those centres was published, which provoked a lot of pressure. "Praljak: Yes. It is somewhat difficult for me to talk about that, because as a Croat, I feel ashamed because of the existence of such things. I am ashamed because they existed. I cannot accept that we consider that a normal thing. There has never been a war or an army which, if they had to put somebody in a detention camp of some kind, not to set such camps up. That is something that exists. You have to put a prisoner of war somewhere, if there are many of them. And Herceg-Bosna was not preparing to have any prisoners of war, nor did it think that there would be a conflict with the Muslims, nobody was rationally prepared for it. At one point, we had to react very quickly, because it was literally a matter of hours as to who would disarm whom. And if you're faced with a situation in which you can either react by disarming your enemy or be disarmed, and thus really lose everything, I do not think that we would recover from that so well. I am prepared to accept responsibility for the decision to disarm them once it all started, because there was no more trust left, and it was too dangerous to wait and risk -- take the risk. So I am prepared to take responsibility for the decision on disarming in Livno, Prozor, Vakuf, et cetera. But I'm not prepared to accept responsibility for what the camps were like."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, General, we're going to talk about the camps later. I want to focus on the passage here, where here you've accepted responsibility for the decision to disarm them once it all started. So, General, the fact is that you did know of and approve of the decision to disarm, at the very least, HVO Muslim members after the events of 30 June, correct, despite what you've been telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is 1995. I was informed about the facts as they occurred, and in an explanation of the overall situation to a journalist, I say to him I could accept, and I was speaking on behalf ultimately of the people sitting there and the HZ-HB, using the conditional tense. And I go on to explain exactly what I mean; that as a Croat, I was ashamed and I am ashamed about what happened over there. And said that here, too. I told you that here, too, and that we can accept General Petkovic's decision under such circumstances to isolate people, given the circumstances and the situation. And then to the best of my knowledge in 1995, because that's the year we're talking about, 1995, that in those detention centres things happened which one can be ashamed of. But I don't see how I could take on responsibility, as far as my subsequent work. So I stand by my words there, I confirm them, with the proviso of the fact that it was 1995, and I always -- I was always talking to the journalist. I said, In the name of everybody, on behalf of everybody. I can't say, Look at this document, look at that. That's that kind of programme, it's that kind of broadcast. Yes, I apologise for rushing on like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you interpreted it wrongly. The facts are as I have described them, and I stand by the words that I've uttered here. They are proper, correct, humane. The only thing is that I'm not naming names, but I use the conditional tense and speak in the name of everybody; what can be accepted, and why, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move to the next exhibit, unless there are questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had a question. I would like to go back to document P3455. So we have this document before us. General Praljak, I'm going to put to you another question, not dealing with prisoners. It is a document from Mr. Petkovic from the 14th of July. We know that you are not there, so I have this in mind. And I would like you to look at the first paragraph. Petkovic is talking to Siljeg and is asking to urgently give targets to XY. I would like to know, in military terms, how you understand or analyse this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't see that sentence. It's completely illegible. I cannot read what it says there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, you are right. In your language, it doesn't appear, and in the English version, it does appear, so I don't quite know how translators have managed. So I withdraw my question because it is true that on the document I can see that it is very difficult for you to see anything. And now it's all black, so I don't think that we see any better. Mr. Stringer, you can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for getting up, Mr. Stringer, but I have to ask how this document was translated if the Croatian text is illegible. That can only mean one of two things: either that there is a legible copy, that there was a legible copy which was not put up on e-court, or that the first sentence was composed, fabricated. But I believe that there was probably a legible copy which we did not get.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll see if we can provide a more legible copy to all parties, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit in the binder is P03794. It's from the 29th of July, 1993, so now we've moved into the period of time after you've taken command of the HVO Main Staff. And here, this is a report submitted by the assistant chief for security, Mr. Tucak, and this report is going to the chief of the military police, Mr. Coric, personally. And it's about his inspection of the Dretelj Barracks on the 27th of July, at which time there were 1.699 detainees in the prisons within the barracks compound, 53 being held separately because they were taken prisoner during an attack on HVO units, 6 religious officials. Security is satisfactory. It says the conditions are rather good for wartime conditions. It says five prisoners have died in the prison. Three were killed while trying to break down the entrance door, and the other two died of natural causes, probably a heart attack. General, now, at this period, 29 July, I take it from what you've said before that you did not have knowledge that there were 1.699 detainees held at the Dretelj Barracks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General Petkovic never told you about this when he handed over the command to you on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic, also to the best of my knowledge, had nothing to do with the detention centres. And this wasn't sent to General Petkovic, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is whether General Petkovic informed you of detainees at Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that Petkovic knew --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Mr. Stringer is putting forward a question of which he presumes -- to which he presumes the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, did you ever learn about these prisoners from Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss any prisoners with Mr. Coric during the time you were commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Coric never -- well, did you have any meetings or discussions with Mr. Coric about other matters during the time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not manage, unfortunately, to attend any such meetings for the reasons I have stipulated here. I don't know whether that was discussed at the meetings or not. I do not know whether there were any meetings in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You talked about this issue on subordination of military police units to the Main Staff, on your request, in order to respond to the ABiH offensive. In connection with that issue, did you have any discussions with Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And apart from that, just the Light Assault Battalion was subordinated to me and part of the military police, not the main portion, the basic part, but the part of the military police of the operative battalion who were trained for dealing with a serious disrupture [as interpreted] of law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P04260.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to have that document, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's my mistake. I've just lost my place in the outline. We were just looking at 3794. The next exhibit would be 3831, 3831, and this is 31 July 1993. This is a Markesic report to the SIS, Operative Zone North-Western Herzegovina commander, North-West Herzegovina Rama Brigade. And in the second paragraph, he writes: "The Rama Brigade SIS is taking certain measures that fall within its domain, and, in accordance with an order from a higher level, is taking into custody all men of Muslim ethnicity aged between 16 and 60 years. As a result, a large number of them were taken to prisons in Ljubuski and Capljina, while 174 of them remained in the Prozor Prison and are being used for work in the field (fortification of defence lines and the like)." Now, General, this is now a week after you've taken command of the HVO Main Staff. Do you know what the order from a higher level is that Mr. Markesic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were aware, or were you not, that at this time they were taking into custody all Muslim -- all men of Muslim ethnicity between ages 16 and 60?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information in that regard, none at all. You see how many people arrived from Bugojno, what the elevations were that had fallen, and then the BH Army nearly smashed the command facility to smithereens. As you see towards the end of the document, two tanks were destroyed. I'm telling you about military issues. As for anything else, I had no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It says that -- well, you said that once you took command of the HVO Main Staff, you raced up to Gornji Vakuf because the situation in that area was -- required your attention; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you were physically present within the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone has 200 kilometres of line from Livno on, and I was along the lines near Gornji Vakuf, going from one -- the focal point of the fighting to the other, which the report reflects. How close were the BH Army and what their artilleries was -- are -- they destroyed a system and two tanks outside the Rama Command, a military policeman was killed. Now you should know what the military situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we know that you spent a good deal of your time during August and September of 1993 in the Prozor-Rama area; correct? That was the focus for you, based on the division of labour you've told us about with General Petkovic, Brigadier -- or General Tole; correct? Prozor-Gornji Vakuf was your area of responsibility or your primary focus?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, yes, but by no means the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the prison that's referred to here, where was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you don't know about any prisons in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 3958, P03958, dated the 5th of August, 1993. This is a different place. This relates to the Dretelj prison facility. Again, General, I think I know what the answer is, but would it be your testimony that you were not aware of 1.835 detainees at the military police barracks in Dretelj, as is indicated here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this report is directed to the Knez Domagoj Brigade. You see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the Knez Domagoj Brigade is a part of the chain of command of the Main Staff, correct, falling within the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the chain; the Main Staff, the operative zone, the brigade. Why did the brigade ask to have a report delivered to it? I don't know. Why they needed that, I don't know. Who it was dispatched to, I don't know. One thing is certain, I received no word on that. And reports are fundamental, who is responsible to whom, who is doing what, and to what extent information is being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, General, I want to take a little more time today to talk about some other events that were taking place during this period of time. We're now in August of 1993. The next exhibit is P09933. And for the record, Mr. President, this is a Rule 92 bis statement that's been admitted into evidence partially, and I'm only going to refer to the parts that have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, the witness's name needs to be removed from the screen. It's a protected witness with a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, we need an order. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But I'm informed that the statement itself is not confidential, so that we can refer to this in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I just want to use this as a basis to ask you about your knowledge of events that were happening in the Capljina-Stolac area during August of 1993. And just to get into this, if you could look at paragraph 19 of this, which is on page 5, page 5 of your version, General, paragraph -- it's the first full paragraph on page 5. Do you have that? The witness begins by saying: "On 23 August 1993 ..."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: She says: "On 23 August 1993, a day I'll never forget, at around 1300 hours, a civilian covered truck and three civilian cars of varying colours drew up near our building. A man in civilian clothes with a megaphone got of the cars. Using it, he announced that all of the Muslim citizens had to leave their apartments and collect near the lorry in the courtyard." And, again, this is in Capljina. And then in this statement, the witness goes on to describe what happened. The people were transported by lorry to the silos, a place she calls the silos, this is in paragraph 23: "... where there was already a mass of people." She said she recognised a lot of people from Capljina. And then the statement continues on. The people had to give up their money. They were then -- she says, and this is paragraph 28 -- and I know yours is not numbered, General. I'm going to go to the paragraph that begins with the words: "I got together all my belongings in my bags." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: " ... and in going outside, passed near to the boxes, but didn't put anything inside. Outside, there was a line of lorries and buses stretching from the silos as far as the Pajdina [phoen] Restaurant, and that is several hundred metres. There were both civilian and military vehicles, and amongst them I recognised a lorry with a red cabin which belonged to a man from Tasavici [phoen]." And it continues on, and it basically talks about how all these people were loaded on all these trucks, and they were then taken out of Capljina on all of these buses. So, General, this is a fairly significantly-sized logistical operation, getting a lot of trucks and lorries together, moving the Muslim population out of Capljina. Were you aware of this taking place on or about the 23rd of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It talks here about the civilians who came and all of that. No, I know nothing about this development. I have no information indicating who organised this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- how it came about in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us during an earlier part of your testimony that you and Mr. Stojic were in Capljina or Stolac on the 15th of August, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I said, and it's not correct. I said that on the 15th of August, I was involved in the fighting in the south of Mostar, around Blagaj, on two different hills. The names are of no consequence. On the 15th, I was with Mr. Stojic after I had returned and after we had succeeded in, for the most part, regaining the positions previously occupied by the BH Army. On account of those attacks, there was a serious obstacle to the delivery of humanitarian aid to Mostar. Mr. Stojic collapsed right in front of me. This was on the 15th of August, the Vela Gospa, the religious festivity in Croatia, the holiday. I tried to sprinkle some cold water to freshen him up, but I think he was then taken to hospital, as far as I remember, simply because he felt sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So in mid-August, you were -- what is precisely the location where you were with Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in Citluk, in the Main Staff building. I was back from the front-line, and Mr. Stojic came to that room, my room or someone's room. It's not like I had a room of my own there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during this period in August of 1993, you did go down to the command post at Citluk; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as I said, on the 15th -- on the 15th, for a while. Whether I was still there an hour later, that's got nothing to do with it. I described this particular event on the 15th. It could have been on or about noon that day, right about midday. I was back from the front-line position, and Mr. Stojic came. I told you the rest, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we know that throughout this period of August, I'm going to put to you, the Muslim population, the women and children, because the men had already been arrested and taken away, the remaining Muslim population in Stolac and Capljina were, as is indicated here for Capljina, rounded up by the HVO and evicted from their homes. Isn't that what happened in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But, sir, what it says here is two persons in civilian clothes came, and then, likewise, it says that the persons who came in civilian clothes -- and then a man got out of a car, again three civilian cars. Capljina was under civilian control. The front-lines facing the Serbs were in Stolac, and whatever went on in Capljina had nothing to do with the responsibility of the Main Staff, unless some renegade members did something or other. But that was certainly a matter for the civilian police, the mayor of that town, the military police if they were soldiers. But I'm not aware of anything like that going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In fact, for there to be lorries and trucks extending a couple of hundred metres, as the witness indicates here, it's not just a small operation, as you've indicated, renegade members. In fact, this would have to be a well-organised logistical operation in order to remove all of those Muslims from Capljina. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that would have required. The document says what it says. It started, apparently, with some civilians who did what this lady describes they did. I am unable to comment because I don't know. But I can set the record straight on what you are suggesting. She's talking about civilians, first and foremost, and then she goes on to refer to some --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General. Well, the fact is that during your watch, during the time that you were commander at the HVO Main Staff, the Muslim population in Stolac was entirely evicted and cleansed out of Stolac; isn't that true? Stolac went from a relative majority Muslim municipality to a municipality where there were no Muslims living there by the time of October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I had no idea about any developments in Stolac throughout my time as commander, the simple reason being Stolac was not a priority in terms of BH Army attacks. I'm not aware of the fact that, except for the town of Stolac itself -- I think Stolac had maybe a small percentage of Muslims, but -- now that you come to mention these terms such as "majority" and "minority," but I never received any information on those developments for the reasons that I mentioned. Stolac could not have been the focus of my attention or time or passion or energy that I needed to expend for other more pressing issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to move you to another exhibit in the binder, P10958. This is an interview that you gave, 10958. General, this is an interview that you gave that was published in "Novi List" on the 4th of April, 2004 [Realtime transcript read in error "1994"], and you're talking about the allegations that are contained in the indictment in this case that had been just made public. And I want to direct you to some comments you made about Stolac. This is page 5 of the English, and in your version, General, it's in the box that says: "In Stolac, some things I sign, but some not." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Mr. Stringer, but the transcript reflects that this is an interview given on the 4th of April, 1994. If you look at the document, it is clear that we're talking about 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thanks for the correction. This is obviously -- or I misspoke, obviously. It's 4th of April, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It says: "In Stolac, some things I sign, but some not." And you're talking about Stolac.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at this. It may be that we've got a bad copy of this, Mr. President. All right, I'm going to come back to this, then, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's illegible, Mr. Stringer, because we're talking about this box over here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll get -- we'll find a better copy and come back to that. Mr. President, I'm just about ready to move to the next binder, but we will need to distribute those, and what I'd propose is perhaps I can -- if we could break early today by ten minutes. I could find a better copy of this article, and we could start with that tomorrow and then continue with the next binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, very well, especially since there's a sitting after us, and so we have to lug two binders. That's heavy enough. I don't think we want to lug a third one. That might be a bit too much for us. So we'll resume tomorrow. You will be talking about binder 8, because we still have one outstanding document in this one, and then we'll start with the next one. Is that it? Yes, thank you. Well, we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m., and I wish you all a pleasant afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25
